nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs § text#1

content.markdown: This document serves as an updated architecture review for the billing team, specifically addressing the selection of a queue for background jobs. It supersedes a previous draft shared via chat, indicating a formalization of the discussion.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Selection criteria § text#0

content.markdown: This section outlines the criteria for selecting an option, categorizing them into must-haves and weighted criteria for scoring.

nodes.title: Must-Have Criteria
nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Selection criteria § text#1

content.markdown:
- No job is lost when a worker crashes or the service is deployed.
- The queue absorbs 1,800 jobs per minute (three times today's peak) without manual intervention.

nodes.title: Weighted Criteria
nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Selection criteria § text#2

content.markdown:
- Operational effort: 40%
- Monthly cost: 30%
- Developer experience, including local testing: 20%
- Portability away from our cloud provider: 10%

content.takeaway: Choose based on operational cost, idempotency needs, and transactional guarantees.

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Options ⨁ Choosing a queue for background jobs › Benefits and trade-offs § table#0

rows: A queue service run by our cloud provider. We send messages to it and workers poll for them; the provider handles storage, scaling and redelivery.
A message broker cluster of three virtual machines that we install, patch and monitor ourselves.
A `jobs` table in the existing billing Postgres database. Workers claim rows with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and mark them done.
Adds read load to the primary database (main risk at month-end)
Move to a dead-letter queue automatically
At least once (requires idempotent job handlers; today only email handler is)
Job can never be lost between commit and enqueue (only covers jobs created inside billing database transaction; not jobs enqueued by reporting service)
Ties us to one provider's API
Needs an emulator that does not support dead-lettering
Priority queues, delayed delivery (month-end invoices can jump ahead of webhook retries)
No one on the team has run this broker in production

nodes.title: Key Differences and Considerations
nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Options ⨁ Choosing a queue for background jobs › Benefits and trade-offs § text#0

content.markdown: Option A offers the lowest operational overhead but requires all job handlers to be idempotent, which is a significant development effort. Option B provides advanced queuing features but comes with a substantial operational burden and a lack of team experience. Option C offers strong transactional guarantees for jobs within the billing database but introduces read load on the primary database and doesn't extend to other services.

content.markdown: The catch is that the service delivers each message at least once, so every job handler must be made idempotent before we switch; today only the email handler is.

nodes.title: Cost Analysis
nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Costs § text#1

content.markdown: The Database job table is the cheapest option for infrastructure, but the Self-hosted broker requires the most team effort. The Managed cloud queue's cost scales with volume, becoming the most expensive at three times current volume.

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Decision status § text#0

content.markdown: This note does not recommend an option. The decision is deferred until Option C has been measured at 1,800 jobs per minute on a production-sized database. Until then, each option carries an open requirement:

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Decision status § text#1

content.markdown:
- Option A: every job handler made idempotent.
- Option B: a named owner for broker on-call and upgrades.
- Option C: a passing load test at 1,800 jobs per minute.

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Context § group#0

content.label: Context
content.takeaway: Current in-process worker pool loses jobs on deploy/crash, causing customer impact during peak loads.

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Context § text#0

content.markdown:
- The billing service processes approximately 40,000 background jobs daily.
- These jobs include rendering invoice PDFs, sending receipt emails, and retrying failed webhooks.
- Currently, jobs run in an in-process worker pool.
- A deploy or crash results in the loss of queued but unstarted jobs.
- Last quarter, 37 invoice emails were lost due to this issue, requiring customers to re-request them.
- Peak load reaches 600 jobs per minute during the month-end billing run.

nodes.title: Also in the source
nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Context § text#1

content.markdown: Today they run in an in-process worker pool, so a deploy or a crash loses any job that was queued but not yet started.

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Evidence § group#0

content.label: Evidence
content.takeaway: Option C load test shows limits; A and B lack internal validation.

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Evidence § text#0

content.markdown:
- **Option C Load Test Results:**
 - Sustained 1,200 jobs per minute with a p95 claim latency of 18 ms on a staging database copy with synthetic jobs.
 - At 2,000 jobs per minute, primary CPU reached 85% and p95 latency rose to 240 ms.
 - 1,800 jobs per minute was not tested.
 - Staging copy is approximately a quarter of production size, so results may not be directly transferable.

nodes.stableKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Evidence § text#1

content.markdown:
- **Options A and B Load Test Status:**
 - Not load-tested.
 - Provider documentation for Option A indicates throughput far above our peak, but this is a third-party figure.
